ITEM 2 — gas-delivery-charge-vs-supply-charge sourcing: CONFIRMED deficient (zero 'sources:' in frontmatter — verified in full-file read; 3,118 words, 10 inline company attributions incl. Natural Gas Advisors, Citizens Utility Board, Localsyr). Company claims: (a) National Grid 'delivery regardless of supplier' — plausible, UNVERIFIED; (b) NIPSCO 'delivery varies with usage + fixed monthly service fee' — consistent with typical tariffs, UNVERIFIED; (c) Con Edison 'embedded taxes…make up nearly a quarter of the delivery charge' — matches ConEd's historical NYC messaging ('about one quarter of delivery charges are local taxes'), still UNVERIFIED at source; (d) Columbia Gas of Ohio '$3.25 per Mcf ($0.325/Ccf) for the 2025–2026 delivery year…added to the monthly NYMEX settlement price to create the total default service rate' — FLAGS: $/Mcf adder + NYMEX-plus structure matches Ohio's Standard Choice Offer (SCO), which is a SUPPLY mechanism, not a delivery charge; if so the page miscategories it (a supply adder used as a delivery-rate example, twice: in body and worked example). Also the Localsyr quote is an electricity-market statistic (share of NY electricity generated by gas) deployed to explain gas-price spikes — tangential. Both need re-derivation at Columbia Gas of Ohio's rate-comparison page and coned.com.

ITEM 3 — 44-how-to-lower-water-bill EPA figures: REFUTED (core), CONFIRMED (context). Fetched https://www.epa.gov/watersense/start-saving 2026-08-29: full text contains NO '30–40%' and NO statement that habits cut indoor use 30–40%; the only 30% on the page is outdoor share ('nearly 9 billion gallons, or 30 percent, is devoted to outdoor water use…as high as 70 percent'). Fetched https://www.epa.gov/watersense/fixaleak 2026-08-29: 'The average household's leaks can account for more than 9,300 gallons of water wasted every year' and 'Fixing easily corrected household water leaks can save homeowners about 10 percent on their water bills' — no $200 figure, no family-of-four dollar framing, no 'up to $200'. Fetched https://www.epa.gov/watersense/statistics-and-facts 2026-08-29: '9,400 gallons…annually from household leaks'; 'We can all use at least 20 percent less water by installing water-efficient fixtures and appliances' (20%, fixtures — the nearest real anchor to 44's 30–40% claim). 44's $500-retrofit/$1,300-per-year pair IS confirmed verbatim on Start Saving ('The average family spends $1,300 per year in water costs, but can save $500 from retrofitting with WaterSense labeled fixtures and ENERGY STAR certified appliances'). DEFECT: 44's inline citation 'available at epa.gov/watersense/fix-leak' is a live 404 (HTTP 404 on fetch 2026-08-29) — dead inline URL violates the site's dead-source standard. Required fix: replace '30–40% indoor habits' with EPA's actual language (~10% leak savings; ~20% via efficient fixtures) and either re-derive 'up to $200' as a labeled site estimate per EPA's 10%-of-bill framing or drop the attribution.

ITEM 4 — 12's winter '80–150 therms': UNVERIFIED externally / REFUTED as attributed. EIA RECS fetch blocked (budget exhausted after eia.gov probes). Structural fact: RECS publishes ANNUAL household end-use data — a monthly winter range cannot be a RECS statistic, so citation [4] (RECS 2020 CE5.2/CE5.4) cannot support '80–150 therms' as attributed regardless of whether the number is defensible. Site-internal contradictions confirm the band is editorial, not sourced: 07-gas-bill-too-high's own table totals 200 therms in the heating month (vs 45 baseline) and uses '120 therms/month in winter'; mcf-vs-ccf-vs-therms says '100–150 CCF in a winter month' (≈104–155 therms) and '20–40 CCF summer' (≈21–41 therms) vs 12's '10–30 therms' summer. Correct framing to install: anchor on annual/seasonal EIA data by climate zone and heating fuel, e.g. 'gas-heated homes in cold climates typically peak near 100–200 therms in the deepest winter months and fall to roughly 10–40 therms in summer (water heating + cooking); what matters for review is your own same-month comparison' — then reconcile 12, 07, and mcf to ONE table and cite the EIA end-use tables as annual context only.

ITEM 5 — why-did-my-utility-bill-go-up 0s TOP: CONFIRMED with precise mechanism. File's first 40 lines: frontmatter has NO hero_above and NO hero_below_answer flag; Quick Answer opens with narration ('You open the bill, see a higher total, and think, "Nothing changed."') with the actionable sentence deferred to paragraph 2. layouts/_default/single.html (project-level, verified): render order = breadcrumbs → header (badge/H1/author/date/min-read meta/description) → collapsed TOC → hero-image partial → body; hero-image.html emits a 1600×900 eager, fetchpriority-high img; site-overrides.css .hero-figure-frame/.hero-img force 'max-height: none; aspect-ratio: auto; object-fit: contain' (full editorial ratio, no crop). why-did-my's hero file is 143,238 bytes. ITEM 6 — 50-best-smart-plugs Emporia outdoor claim: UNVERIFIED (fetch budget exhausted; search backend returned token-garbage thesaurus/serp results on 3 attempts). Repo facts hard-verified: line 80 of 50-best-smart-plugs-standby-power.md asserts 'Outdoor rated | Yes (weather-resistant)' for the Emporia Smart Plug, and the frontmatter sources list (DOE FEMP, betterbuildingssolutioncenter, energystar, wikipedia, kasasmart KP115, tp-link Tapo) contains NO emporiaenergy.com URL — the one row unique to Emporia is the one row with no manufacturer source on file. Emporia's homepage (fetched 2026-08-29) confirms a 'Smart Plugs' product line exists but does not state ratings. Known-risk note (labeled as domain knowledge, not verification): Emporia ships distinct indoor and OUTDOOR smart-plug SKUs; the standard plug is generally not outdoor-rated, so if the table's row refers to the standard plug/ASIN B0CLVV7X7Y, the cell is likely wrong or conflates two products. Re-derivation instruction: fetch the emporiaenergy.com smart-plug product page + spec sheet (shop.emporiaenergy.com) and check both SKUs' ratings before shipping any edit.

ITEM 7 — 16-budget-billing 100% bounce: CONFIRMED (cause-consistent; every structural marker present). hero_below_answer:true suppresses the hero, so the first screen is purely header + Quick Answer — and that QA is two paragraphs of pure defensive meta ('…must be confirmed in the serving utility's written plan terms. / Do not assume that a plan removes charges, guarantees a stable payment…') with NO number, NO mechanism, NO example. The defensive-QA-first pattern also explains why THIS page bounced 100% while 43 (also defensive, but with a table) is 100% br at 0s and 24 (same genre, same structure) shows a 4s TOP — 16's QA is the most answer-empty of the set.

The hub (922 words/6,943 bytes, TOP 206s but 90.9% br) is a WORKFLOW page whose Quick Answer explicitly disclaims the data intent ('starts with your own account records, NOT national average costs or a generic line-item table').
